claims.text: The proposed hybrid method combines machine-learning regression with a physics-informed defect-scattering correction.
The machine-learning component is trained on both perfect-crystal data and defect-inclusive simulation results.
The hybrid method will predict thermal conductivity more accurately than conventional perfect-crystal analytical models in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The hybrid method will predict electronic conductivity more accurately than conventional perfect-crystal analytical models in both temperature regimes.
The target specimen is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
Quantum effects are pronounced in the 0–200 K regime.
Defect scattering is pronounced in the 0–200 K regime.
Transport in the 300–1200 K regime is phonon-dominated.
Oxygen impurity affects high-temperature transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Defects and oxygen dopant sites act as scattering centers that alter lattice vibrations.
Defects and oxygen dopant sites alter electron and phonon transport.
The method uses high-fidelity atomistic simulations that explicitly include defects and impurities.
The method uses experimental measurements to inform the machine-learning model.
Explicit treatment of defect-induced scattering corrects traditional Boltzmann-transport predictions.
Learning from ideal and non-ideal behavior bridges the gap between theoretical predictions and real-sample performance.
The accuracy improvement will be greatest in the 0–200 K regime because defect effects are unusually dominant there.
Existing analytical approaches assume perfect crystals and neglect explicit defect and impurity scattering.
The stated applicability domain is HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen near 1 wt.% over 0–1200 K.
Significantly different oxygen levels or other alloy systems may require model recalibration.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in prediction error relative to the baseline across both temperature ranges would falsify the hypothesis.
